definition: The setting in which ideas are produced (supplied) and received (demanded); in Mokyr's account shaped by political fragmentation.
Knowledge, from scientific insight to practical know-how, that fuels innovation and growth.
Knowledge of why things work: the science behind a technique.
Knowledge of how to do things: techniques and recipes.
Innovation displacing old technologies and firms; threatened by protectionism.
The 17th–18th century intellectual movement in Western Europe that snowballed into the Industrial Revolution.
Publishing and openly debating new ideas so they spread rapidly; rewarded by priority credit, not profit.
How politically fragmented a region is: high in Europe, low in unified China.
The demand side of the market for ideas; falls as fragmentation rises.
The supply side of the market for ideas; persecution is less effective as fragmentation rises, so more ideas are supplied.
The transnational community of European scholars that gave fragmented states a unified market for ideas.
A good one person can use without reducing what is available to others, like knowledge.
Recognition for being first to an idea: the reward in open science.
The extra cost of producing one more unit.
The extra revenue from selling one more unit; for P = 339 − Q it is 339 − 2Q.
A market with a single seller, which sets output where MR = MC and charges the price on the demand curve.
Firms colluding to act as one monopolist and split output and profit.
Oligopolists set prices; with identical products they undercut down to P = MC.
Oligopolists choose output simultaneously without colluding.
A leader chooses output first, anticipating the follower's reaction function.
A firm's profit-maximising output given its belief about the rival's output, e.g. q_G = 96 − ½q_U.
The Bertrand outcome with identical products: price equals marginal cost and profit is zero, as under competition.
The value consumers enjoy from paying less than they were willing to; the area under demand above price.
What producers receive from selling units at a price above marginal cost.
Surplus lost to everyone because output is below the competitive level.
Price times quantity, P × Q: 28,224 under Bertrand down to 23,328 under collusion.
Strategies from which no player can gain by changing only their own strategy.
A probability distribution over actions, used to avoid being predictable.
Playing one action with certainty.
In a mixed equilibrium, each player's probabilities make the opponent's expected payoffs from their two actions equal.
A variable the model sets out to explain, such as real GDP or investment.
A variable the model takes as given, such as the saving rate.
Multiplying all inputs by z multiplies output by z: zY = F(zK, zL).
y = f(k): output per worker as a function of capital per worker, possible because of constant returns to scale.
The extra output from one more unit of capital per worker; the slope of f(k), which diminishes as k rises.
The constant fraction s of income saved and invested; i = s·f(k).
The constant fraction δ of capital that wears out each year.
The capital per worker k* at which investment equals break-even investment, so Δk = 0.
A change in the steady-state level of income per person but not its growth rate; the effect of higher saving.
A change in the steady-state growth rate of income per person.
The steady-state capital per worker that maximises consumption per worker; MPK = δ.
The investment needed to keep k constant: (δ + n + g)k.
The constant rate n at which the labour force grows.
E in Y = F(K, L × E): society's knowledge of production methods, growing at rate g.
L × E: the number of workers adjusted for the efficiency of labour.
Technology modelled as growth in the efficiency of labour, so it acts like more workers.
